privacyPolicyPage.title: Privacy Policy
privacyPolicyPage.introP1: This Privacy Policy applies to the Seekprotocol mobile application (referred to throughout this document as "the Application"), developed and maintained by Block Protocol LLC (referred to as "the Service Provider") as a free service for mobile devices. The Application is provided on an "AS IS" basis.
privacyPolicyPage.introP2: Seekprotocol is a next-generation augmented reality, AI-powered, and blockchain-integrated platform that creates gamified real-world experiences for its users. Given the nature of these experiences, the Application interacts with several categories of personal data in order to deliver its features fully and safely. This policy describes in complete detail what data is collected, why it is collected, how it is handled, with whom it may be shared, and the rights available to users with respect to their personal information.
privacyPolicyPage.introP3: By downloading and using the Application, you consent to the data practices described in this Privacy Policy. This policy should be reviewed regularly, as it may be updated from time to time to reflect changes in data practices, applicable laws, or Application features.
privacyPolicyPage.part1Title: Part I: Information Collection and Use
privacyPolicyPage.part1P1: The Application collects information when you download and use it. This includes technical data gathered automatically during use, such as your device's Internet Protocol (IP) address, the pages or sections of the Application you visit, the time and date of your visits, the duration of time spent on those pages, and information about the operating system running on your mobile device.
privacyPolicyPage.part1P2: Beyond this automatically collected technical data, the Application collects several categories of personal information, each described in full below.
privacyPolicyPage.part1P3: All data collected by the Application is transmitted and stored using encryption in transit, ensuring that information is protected as it travels between your device and the Service Provider's systems.
privacyPolicyPage.part1s1P1: The Application supports multiple methods for users to create and access their accounts. These include username and password authentication, username combined with other forms of authentication, username combined with both password and additional authentication factors, and OAuth-based authentication through supported external identity providers. The account creation method used by a given user determines which account-related identifiers are collected and retained by the Application.
privacyPolicyPage.part1s2P1: The Application collects personally identifiable information including your name, email address, and user identifiers (User IDs).
privacyPolicyPage.part1s2P2: Your name is collected because it is required to support core app functionality, including personalizing the user interface and identifying your profile within the platform. This data is collected only and is not shared with third parties.
privacyPolicyPage.part1s2P3: Your email address is similarly required and is collected exclusively to support app functionality, including account authentication, service-related communications, and the delivery of important notices. This data is collected only and is not shared with third parties.
privacyPolicyPage.part1s2P4: User IDs, the unique identifiers assigned to your account or session, are required and are collected for a broader set of purposes. These include supporting core app functionality, conducting internal analytics to understand how the Application is used, enforcing security and fraud prevention measures, and managing account-level features and permissions. User IDs are collected only and are not shared externally.
privacyPolicyPage.part1s3P1: The Application requires access to both approximate and precise location data from your device. Location access is mandatory and cannot be disabled by users without affecting core app functionality.
privacyPolicyPage.part1s3P2: Approximate location data, identifying your general geographic area without pinpointing your exact position, is both collected and shared. It is collected to support core app functionality and to conduct internal analytics regarding how users engage with location-based features across different geographic regions. Approximate location data is also shared with third parties for the purposes of supporting app functionality and providing personalized content and experiences based on geographic context.
privacyPolicyPage.part1s3P3: Precise location data, meaning exact geographic coordinates derived from GPS or equivalent technologies, is both collected and shared, and it serves the broadest range of purposes of any data type in the Application. This reflects the fact that Seekprotocol's core experience is built around real-world, location-anchored augmented reality. Precise location data is collected to support AR features and other core functionality that depends on exact real-world positioning, to conduct detailed usage analytics, to transmit developer communications relevant to your specific location, to apply security and fraud prevention measures tied to geographic activity patterns, to personalize content and features to your precise environment, and to manage account features or service conditions that depend on geographic parameters. This same data is shared with third-party service providers for all of these same purposes.
privacyPolicyPage.part1s4P1: The Application collects three forms of messaging data: emails, SMS or MMS messages, and other in-app messages. All three types are required and cannot be disabled by the user.
privacyPolicyPage.part1s4P2: Emails are collected exclusively to support core app functionality, including communication between users and the platform and the delivery of service-related notifications.
privacyPolicyPage.part1s4P3: SMS or MMS data is collected solely to support core app functionality and is processed ephemerally, meaning it is not retained after the relevant processing task is complete and is not stored persistently by the Application.
privacyPolicyPage.part1s4P4: Other in-app messages are collected exclusively to support core app functionality, including interactions within the Application's own messaging and communication systems.
privacyPolicyPage.part1s5P1: The Application requires access to photos and videos on your device. Both data types are collected only and are used exclusively to support core app functionality, particularly in the context of augmented reality features that require access to the device camera and media library for overlaying digital content onto physical environments or capturing experiences within the Application's interactive sessions.
privacyPolicyPage.part1s6P1: The Application collects health-related information and fitness-related information. Both categories are required and are used exclusively to support core app functionality. This data is not shared with third parties.
privacyPolicyPage.part1s6P2: Health information enables the Application to integrate health context into its experiences where relevant, supporting features that respond to a user's general physical condition as part of Seekprotocol's broader gamified engagement model.
privacyPolicyPage.part1s6P3: Fitness information is used in conjunction with the Application's challenge and reward systems. The Application requests the Android ACTIVITY_RECOGNITION permission in order to detect and monitor physical activities such as walking, running, or cycling directly through your device's sensors. This permission powers the Application's challenge and reward features, which are designed to recognize real-world physical activity as part of Seekprotocol's gamified experience. By detecting movement patterns, the Application is able to trigger in-app events, validate challenge completions, and attribute rewards tied to physical engagement in the real world. No activity recognition data is used for advertising purposes, and it is not shared with third parties. This permission may be revoked at any time through your device's application settings, though doing so will disable the activity-based challenges and rewards that depend on it.
privacyPolicyPage.part1s7P1: The Application collects technical data related to its own performance. This includes crash logs, diagnostic information, and other app performance metrics.
privacyPolicyPage.part1s7P2: Crash logs are required and are collected automatically to support core app functionality: specifically, to identify, diagnose, and resolve technical failures that affect the user experience.
privacyPolicyPage.part1s7P3: Diagnostic information and other app performance data are optional and are collected only when users choose to allow them. When collected, this data is used solely to monitor, maintain, and improve the stability and responsiveness of the Application over time.
privacyPolicyPage.part1s8P1: The Application may optionally collect files and documents accessible from your device. This collection is user-controlled and is triggered only in contexts where your direct interaction with the Application involves files or documents. When collected, this data is used solely to support core app functionality and is not shared with third parties.
privacyPolicyPage.part1s9P1: The Application collects device identifiers and similar technical identifiers. This data is required and cannot be disabled. Device identifiers are both collected and shared, and are processed ephemerally, meaning they are used for real-time session handling and are not stored persistently beyond the immediate purpose.
privacyPolicyPage.part1s9P2: Device identifiers are collected for the purposes of supporting core app functionality that depends on device-level recognition and enforcing security and fraud prevention measures. The same data is shared with third parties for app functionality and security and fraud prevention purposes.
privacyPolicyPage.part2Title: Part II: Third-Party Access and Data Sharing
privacyPolicyPage.part2P1: Only aggregated, anonymized data is periodically transmitted to external services to assist the Service Provider in improving the Application and their services. The Service Provider may share your information with third parties in the ways described in this section.
privacyPolicyPage.part2P2: The Application may disclose both user-provided and automatically collected information when required to do so by law, for example in response to a subpoena or similar legal process, or when the Service Provider believes in good faith that disclosure is necessary to protect their rights, protect your safety or the safety of others, investigate fraud, or respond to a government request. Information may also be shared with trusted service providers who work on the Service Provider's behalf, who do not have independent use of the information disclosed to them, and who have agreed to adhere to the rules set forth in this Privacy Policy.
privacyPolicyPage.part2P3: The Application integrates the following third-party services, each of which operates under its own privacy policy. Users are encouraged to review those policies directly to understand how each provider handles data received from the Application:
privacyPolicyPage.part3P1: You may stop all collection of information by the Application at any time by uninstalling it. You may use the standard uninstall processes available on your mobile device or through the applicable mobile application marketplace.
privacyPolicyPage.part3P2: For optional data types, specifically diagnostic information, other app performance data, and files and documents, collection can be controlled within the Application's settings without requiring a full uninstall.
privacyPolicyPage.part3P3: For the ACTIVITY_RECOGNITION permission on Android, this may be revoked at any time through your device's application permissions settings. Revoking this permission will disable activity-based challenges and rewards but will not otherwise affect your use of the Application.
privacyPolicyPage.part4P1: The Service Provider retains user-provided data for as long as you use the Application and for a reasonable period thereafter in order to fulfill legitimate operational, legal, or administrative needs. Data that is processed ephemerally, specifically SMS/MMS data and device identifiers, is not retained beyond the immediate purpose for which it was collected and is discarded at the end of each relevant processing session.
privacyPolicyPage.part4P2: If you would like the Service Provider to delete user-provided data that you have submitted through the Application, please contact them at <email>support@seekprotocol.ai</email>. The Service Provider will respond within a reasonable timeframe.
privacyPolicyPage.part5P1: The Service Provider does not use the Application to knowingly solicit data from or market to children under the age of 13. The Application is not directed at anyone under the age of 13, and the Service Provider does not knowingly collect personally identifiable information from children in that age group. If the Service Provider discovers that a child under 13 has provided personal information, it will be deleted from their servers immediately. If you are a parent or guardian and you believe your child has provided personal information to the Application, please contact the Service Provider at <email>support@seekprotocol.ai</email> so that they may take the necessary corrective action.
privacyPolicyPage.part6P1: The Service Provider is committed to safeguarding the confidentiality and integrity of your information. All data collected by the Application is encrypted in transit. Physical, electronic, and procedural safeguards are maintained to protect the information that the Service Provider processes and retains. Where data is transmitted to third-party service providers, the Service Provider makes reasonable efforts to ensure such sharing is limited, purpose-bound, and subject to appropriate data handling agreements.

privacyPolicyPage.part7P2: Alternatively, deletion requests may be submitted by contacting the Service Provider directly at <email>support@seekprotocol.ai</email>. The Service Provider will process all deletion requests within a reasonable timeframe.

The Service Provider will notify you of any changes by updating this page with the new Privacy Policy and revising the effective date shown at the top of this document. Continued use of the Application following the posting of any changes constitutes your acceptance of those changes.

placed.title: Something is placed
placed.body: A brand, a project or an event pins an asset to a set of coordinates and sets the radius it can be claimed from. It sits there, visible on the map, until someone comes to get it.

arrive.title: You walk into range
arrive.body: Your phone confirms you are actually there: satellite fix, ambient radio, device attestation and your motion trace all have to agree. Spoofing one signal is easy; spoofing all of them at once is not.

collect.title: You collect it
collect.meta: Settles on the asset's own chain
collect.body: Hold up the camera, see the asset anchored in the street in front of you, and take it. The transfer settles on-chain for a fraction of a cent, and it is yours.

orbit.label: Orbit
orbit.title: Every drop is a coordinate
orbit.body: Assets are published to points on the planet, not to a feed. From up here that is all the network is: a few thousand places where something is waiting.

descent.label: Descent
descent.title: Falling towards one of them
descent.body: Pick any of those points and go. The protocol does not care which, only that you are standing there when you claim it.

street.label: Street level
street.title: This is the same map, four hundred kilometres closer
street.body: The buildings you are flying over are the ones between you and the drop. Distance is the whole mechanic, so the map has to be the real one.

hand.label: In your hand
hand.title: And it fits in a phone
hand.body: Nothing was swapped out. The view you just flew through is what the app renders, with its own controls over the top.

see.label: The camera looks
see.title: A camera does not see a street
see.body: It sees brightness changing across a grid. Before anything can be placed anywhere, the scene has to be turned into something with structure, and at this point there is none.

track.label: Features resolve
track.title: Corners are what the world is made of
track.body: Points where brightness changes in two directions at once survive movement, so the engine keeps them and throws the rest away. Track enough of them across enough frames and the phone knows how it moved.

plane.label: A plane is found
plane.title: Something to stand on
plane.body: Features that share a surface get grouped into a plane. That is the moment a drop stops being a picture on your screen and becomes an object with a place to sit.

anchor.label: The anchor sets
anchor.title: Pinned to the world, not to the phone
anchor.body: The drop is bound to that patch of geometry and to the coordinate it was published at. Walk around it and it stays where it was. Two people standing in the same place see it in the same spot.

persist.label: It persists
persist.title: Still there tomorrow
persist.body: The anchor is stored against the location rather than the session, so closing the app does not move it. That persistence is what separates an AR toy from an AR protocol.

mobiSection.title: The companion that can see what you see
mobiSection.lead: Ask out loud and Mobi reads the street through the camera: landmarks, opening hours, which way the drop is. It runs on-device wherever it can, and it never keeps a trace of where you have been.
points: Voice in, voice out, hands free while you walk

socialSection.lead: Clans pool what everyone collects. Chat is end-to-end encrypted, with disappearing messages when a conversation should not outlive itself. And bringing someone in earns you a share of what they find.

featureGroups.title: More than a map with coins on it

items.title: Spawns on real coordinates
items.body: Drops appear at fixed points around you and stay there until someone claims them. Mark one and the app counts down the distance as you walk.

items.title: Persistent AR catches
items.body: The coin anchors to the ground in front of you and stays anchored between sessions, so it is in the same spot for everyone who comes to it.

items.title: Power-ups and timing
items.body: Magnet, double and freeze stack on a catch. A timing bar decides how much of the drop you keep, because a legendary caught badly is still a legendary caught badly.

items.title: Rarity that means something
items.body: Common through legendary, with rarity driving the ring colour on the map before you get anywhere near it.

items.title: Ten ranks, earned by walking
items.body: Seeker through Legend. Rank comes from distance covered and places visited, not from what you spent.

items.title: Sixty-one badges
items.body: A full collectible set, from Diamond Hands to On-Chain Detective, each with its own unlock condition.

items.title: Game Center and Play Games
items.body: Achievements sync to the platform you already use, so the streaks and milestones sit alongside the rest of your games.

items.title: Streaks and daily quests
items.body: Missions that adapt to where you are and how you play, with the reward scaling as the streak holds.

items.title: Clans
items.body: Join or found one, pool contributions, and climb the clan table. Emblems, ranks and shared reward pools included.

items.title: Encrypted chat
items.body: Direct and clan messages, end-to-end encrypted, with disappearing messages when a conversation should not outlive itself.

items.title: Leaderboards
items.body: Global, national and clan-level, with medals for the top three and a table that updates as people walk.

items.title: Referrals
items.body: Bring people in and earn a share of what they collect. Your code is the first thing on the screen, because it is what you came for.

items.title: A wallet without a seed phrase
items.body: Created from a social login so you can collect within a minute of installing. Export the key whenever you want custody.

items.title: Seekprotocol Pass
items.body: A season track of rewards that runs alongside normal play, with a free tier and a paid one.

items.title: Shop

items.title: 3D avatars
items.body: Full Decentraland-compatible avatars with animations and emotes, not a cropped profile photo.

progression.lead: Rank comes from distance covered and places visited. Everything on this wall is earned by going outside.

clansSection.lead: Found a clan or join one, pool what everyone collects, and climb the table together. Chat is end-to-end encrypted, and messages can be set to disappear when a conversation should not outlive itself.

collectiblesSection.title: These are the coins out there
collectiblesSection.lead: Rarity decides how often one spawns and how likely you are to keep it. A caught unit is a game unit. What it pays out in real tokens is the market's business.

voucher.label: Discount voucher
voucher.headline: Money off, at the door that gave it to you
voucher.fine: One per person · Valid 14 days · In store only
voucher.redeem: The code is shown at the counter and marked used. It cannot be forwarded, because it was issued to the device that stood inside the radius.
voucher.proof: The claim is on-chain with the coordinate it was taken at, so a redemption can be checked against a real arrival rather than a screenshot.

asset.label: Real world asset
asset.headline: A physical thing, waiting at a place
asset.fine: 1 of 250 · Collect in store · Expires when stock does
asset.redeem: The holder collects the item itself. The token is the claim on it, and it burns at handover so the same pair cannot be collected twice.
asset.proof: Stock is finite and the claim is a lock, not a lookup, so two people reaching for the last one cannot both be told they got it.
asset.placedBy: Brands with something to give away

access.label: Access pass
access.headline: The ticket is being at the venue
access.fine: Non-transferable · Expires at the end of the event
access.redeem: Scanned at the gate like any other pass. The difference is that it could only be obtained on site, which is what makes it worth issuing.
access.proof: High-value drops set a strict confidence threshold, so the radio environment has to agree with the position before it is released.

token.label: Token drop
token.headline: Distribution that costs something to farm
token.fine: One claim per device · Settles on its own chain
token.redeem: It arrives in the wallet the app made for you, and it is yours to hold, move or sell. Nothing to redeem and nobody to ask.
token.proof: A wallet is free to create and a walk is not. Geography is the filter that an airdrop cannot cheaply be farmed through.

collectible.label: Collectible
collectible.headline: Something that only exists where it was placed
collectible.fine: Series of 500 · Tradeable · Rarity fixed at issue
collectible.redeem: Nothing to redeem. It is a record of having been somewhere, which is the oldest reason anybody has ever kept anything.
collectible.proof: Each one carries the coordinate it was taken at, so the set someone holds is a map of where they have actually been.

rewards.title: Anything can be waiting at a coordinate
rewards.lead: A coin is the version everyone pictures, and it is the least interesting one. The protocol does not care what is in the box: if it can be issued to a person it can be issued to a place, and somebody has to walk there to take it.
rewards.phoneAlt: The Seekprotocol app showing a live event and the rewards it is handing out
rewards.participateLabel: Take part in the live event
rewards.alertBody: 301 m away and live until 9 p.m. It goes to whoever reaches it first.
rewards.foundFine: Claimed on arrival and settled on chain. It is in your wallet.
rewards.foundAlt: Winning a reward on the map
rewards.proofNote: Whatever is in the box, what stops it being claimed by someone who was never there is the same: presence, scored against four independent signals at the moment of the claim.

tokens.label: Tokens
tokens.headline: Any token, on any chain
tokens.body: Ethereum, Solana, BNB Smart Chain and the networks after them. A publisher funds a campaign in the token they already hold and it settles where that token lives, so nobody has to bridge anything to take part.

memes.label: Memecoins
memes.headline: The launches nobody has a channel for
memes.body: A memecoin has an audience and no way to reach it that is not an airdrop farm. Putting the supply in real streets sets it in front of people who came out for it, and every claim is a person rather than an address.

nfts.label: NFTs
nfts.headline: Minted where you were standing
nfts.body: A collectible carrying the coordinate it came from is a different object to one minted from a sofa. An edition can be bound to a city, a venue or a single doorway, and the record of where each one was taken is public.

vouchers.label: Vouchers
vouchers.headline: Money off, at the counter
vouchers.body: The format a high street actually wants. A code that only opens inside the doorway, redeemed at the till by somebody who walked in, and counted as an arrival rather than as an impression that might have led to one.

goods.label: Real-world goods
goods.headline: Things that turn up in a box
goods.body: A console, a pair of trainers, a piece of kit. The claim is on chain and the fulfilment is ordinary logistics, which is what lets a brand put something physical at the end of a walk without building anything to do it.

events.label: Live events
events.headline: All of it, for the length of the event
events.body: A festival, a match or a conference becomes a temporary layer of rewards that expires when the event does. Turning up is what unlocks them, so the prize pool reaches the people who were actually there, and the counter is the door.

distribution.title: Reach is easy to buy and impossible to trust
distribution.lead: Every channel a launch can buy sells the same thing: a number a script can produce. Impressions, clicks, follows, wallets, all of them cost a fraction of a cent to manufacture at scale. Presence is the one interaction nobody has automated, because nobody has written a bot that walks.

failures.bots: Paid traffic arrives from data centres and click farms. You pay per impression, and a meaningful share of them were never rendered to a person at all.
failures.farms: An airdrop is claimed by wallets, and a wallet costs nothing. One farmer with a script becomes forty thousand eligible addresses, and the tokens land nowhere near the people they were meant for.
failures.unaudited: Engagement figures are reported by the platform selling them. A follow, a view or a modelled store visit cannot be audited, so the campaign is judged on a number you have to take on faith.

answers.bots: A claim is a device that stood at a coordinate, with its satellite fix, its radio surroundings and its motion trace all agreeing. There is no server-side version of being somewhere.
answers.farms: One claim per device inside the radius and the window. A second claim means a second journey, and nobody is in forty cities at once.
answers.unaudited: Every claim is a public record: a coordinate, a time, an asset. Count them yourself on a block explorer instead of asking us for the figure.

distribution.askLegend: What do you want them to do?
distribution.askNote: The protocol verifies that a person was there. What they have to do to earn the reward is yours to write, and none of it changes the verification underneath.

visit.label: Walk into the shop
visit.headline: Claim at the counter
visit.body: The drop sits inside the doorway with a radius tight enough that only a phone at the till can open it. The code that gets redeemed belongs to someone who came in.
visit.recorded: A verified arrival at your address, timestamped at the moment of the claim.

follow.label: Follow the account
follow.headline: Follow to unlock
follow.body: The asset stays locked until the account is followed, and the follow only counts from a device inside the radius. A farm can produce the follow. It cannot produce the walk.
follow.recorded: A follow that arrived with a verified visit behind it, counted against the location it happened at.

signup.label: Sign up or join the list
signup.headline: Sign up on the spot
signup.body: One field, filled in where the drop is. Every address on the list belongs to a person who was standing at your campaign when they typed it.
signup.recorded: A signup with a verified arrival behind it, which is the only kind worth paying for.

scan.label: Scan the product
scan.headline: Scan it on the shelf
scan.body: Point the camera at the item rather than at a pin. The scan has to happen inside the radius, so the reward reaches the person actually holding the thing.
scan.recorded: A scan of one product at one store, counted per line rather than per campaign.

mint.label: Mint on the spot
mint.headline: Mint where you stand
mint.body: The collectible is minted at the coordinate and carries it. What it is worth later has something to do with where it came from, which a mint page cannot say.
mint.recorded: A mint tied to a place and a moment, on whichever chain the collection lives on.

distribution.dropFine: One claim per device · Verified on arrival
distribution.recordedNever: Counts by location, time and campaign. Never an individual, and never a trace of where they went next.
distribution.chainsNote: A source is anybody who can issue something: a project, a brand, a venue, a shop on the corner. A network is a row in a table rather than a release, so one campaign can run across several at once and a seeker never has to pick one. Ethereum and Solana settle today; the next one is configuration.

walkthrough.title: This is the whole loop
walkthrough.lead: Not a video of the app. These are its own rules, running here. Tap a spawn on the map and take it from there.

map.label: The map
map.title: Everything nearby, standing where it actually is
map.body: Spawns sit on fixed coordinates and stay there until someone claims them. Tap one to see what it is and how far you have to walk.

spawn.label: The spawn
spawn.title: Rarity tells you what you are walking towards
spawn.body: Common through legendary, each with its own catch chance. You get two attempts, and the retry is worth 0.65 of the first, so the opening tap matters most.

catch.label: The catch
catch.title: Tap to charge, and hold your nerve
catch.body: The ring fills as you tap. Something interrupts every round or two: the orb freezes, the charge springs a leak, or a surge opens where taps count double.

result.label: The roll
result.title: Charge buys chance, it does not buy certainty
result.body: A full ring on a legendary is still a one-in-five. That is what makes a legendary worth having, and what makes the tap decide something.

wallet.label: Yours
wallet.title: It lands in a wallet you never had to set up
wallet.body: Created from a social login, so a first-time player collects something within a minute. Export the key whenever you want custody.

spawnScreen.note: Charging the ring raises this. The retry after it is worth 0.65 of the first.

mechanic.freeze: Frozen, keep tapping to melt it

resultScreen.noteCaught: A caught unit is a game unit. What it pays out in real tokens is the market's business.

ecosystemPage.metaDescription: How the Seekprotocol ecosystem fits together: seekers who collect, publishers who place, and the protocol that verifies presence and settles it on chain.
ecosystemPage.lead: Someone places an asset. Someone travels to it. The protocol confirms they were really there and settles it. Everything else is detail on top of that loop.
ecosystemPage.networkTitle: Every pin is a real place
ecosystemPage.networkLead: Drag the globe. The coordinates are genuine city positions, and every arc is a drop moving between them.
ecosystemPage.faqLead: Including the ones with uncomfortable answers.
ecosystemPage.ctaBody: Proof of location, the architecture, the token design, and a straight list of the attacks we defend against and the limits we accept.
ecosystemPage.polCtaBody: Four independent signals must agree before a claim is accepted. The plain-language walkthrough is on the blog.

seekers.label: Seekers
seekers.title: People who go and get it
seekers.body: Anyone with the app. They walk, they find things, and they keep what they collect. No prior crypto knowledge is assumed: the wallet is created from a social login and can be exported later by anyone who wants custody.
gets: Quests that adapt to where they are
A wallet they did not have to understand first

publishers.label: Publishers
publishers.title: Whoever put it there
publishers.body: Brands, venues, token projects and event organisers. They place assets at coordinates they care about and pay per placement, weighted by radius, duration and how contested the area is.
gets: A campaign builder with no integration work

protocol.label: Protocol
protocol.title: The part that keeps them honest
protocol.body: Verification scoring, asset custody and settlement. It takes a fee on placement, routes the majority of it back to seekers, and holds the record of what was claimed where.
gets: Parameters that move to governance over time

placement.title: Geofenced placement
placement.body: Assets are pinned to coordinates with a configurable claim radius. A shop doorway uses a tight radius; a festival ground uses a wide one.

verification.title: Multi-signal verification
verification.body: Satellite fix, ambient radio, device attestation and motion continuity all have to agree before a claim is accepted.

anchoring.title: AR anchoring
anchoring.body: Assets stay put between sessions and between users. Two people standing in the same place see the same thing in the same spot.

companion.title: AI companion
companion.body: Reads the camera to explain what you are looking at and suggest where to go next, without shipping your movement history anywhere.

wallet.title: Social wallet
wallet.body: Created from a social login so a first-time user can collect something within a minute, with self-custody export available whenever they want it.

settlement.title: Multi-chain settlement
settlement.body: An asset settles on the network it already lives on, against one requirement that every chain has to meet: picking up a small reward must not cost more than the reward is worth.

spoofing.question: Can I fake my location to collect without going there?
spoofing.answer: Not cheaply. A raw GPS fix is easy to spoof, which is why it is only one of four signals. The ambient radio environment, device attestation and your motion trace all have to corroborate it, and a device that fails repeatedly faces a higher threshold. The aim is to make forgery cost more than the reward is worth, not to claim it is impossible.

crypto.question: Do I need to know anything about crypto to use Seekprotocol?
crypto.answer: No. The wallet is created from a social login and you never see a seed phrase unless you go looking for one. If you later want self-custody, you can export the key at any point.

tracking.question: Is Seekprotocol tracking where I go?
tracking.answer: No. The app asks for a position when you attempt a claim, not continuously in the background. Raw sensor data is used to score that one claim and then discarded, and your movement history stays on your device.

farming.question: What stops one person farming a location with many wallets?
farming.answer: Per-device claim limits within a radius and time window, plus device attestation that emulator farms fail. Wallets are free but travel is not, which is the point of anchoring distribution to geography in the first place.

chain.question: Which chain does Seekprotocol run on?
chain.answer: Whichever one the asset lives on. Networks are rows in a table rather than code, so a publisher funds a campaign in the token they already hold and a seeker never has to pick a chain. What every network has to meet is the same requirement: a reward worth a few cents has to survive being moved, and someone standing on a street corner should not have to wait for it. The strip on the homepage says which chains settle today.

business.question: Can my business place assets today?
business.answer: Through a managed partnership, yes. The self-serve portal that removes the conversation with us is in progress, and the roadmap says where it sits.

businessPage.metaDescription: Location-based AR advertising for publishers and brands. Place a reward at your coordinates and pay per verified visit, not per impression.
businessPage.lead: Digital advertising can put your logo in front of someone in milliseconds. It cannot get them to walk three streets over. Place a reward at your door and pay for the people who reach it.
businessPage.argumentLead: Spend the same money two ways and the funnels look comparable until the last row. One of them is counted. The other is a model, and it is the row every campaign is judged on.
businessPage.setupLead: This is the whole flow. Make the four choices and publish, and see what each one does to the ground you are holding and the price of a person at your door.
businessPage.measurementTitle: What you get, and what you do not
businessPage.measurementLead: Location data is the most sensitive category there is. You receive the counts you need to judge a campaign, and nothing that would let you follow an individual around.
businessPage.ctaBody: The self-serve portal is in progress. Until it lands, we set campaigns up with you directly. Tell us the location and what you want to place.
businessPage.realTitle: What an arrival is, and what it is not
businessPage.realLead: Every metric on the market is a proxy, and every proxy has a script that produces it for less than a cent. Presence is the exception, and it is the exception for a reason that does not erode with better hardware: the cost is physical.
businessPage.chainsNote: Fund a campaign in the asset you already hold, wherever it lives. A network is configuration rather than an integration, so one campaign can run across several at once and the person claiming never has to know which.
businessPage.verifiedTitle: Pay only when someone was actually there
businessPage.verifiedBody: No impressions, no clicks that never became a visit. A campaign spends when the protocol has verified a person on-site.

retail.title: Turn a location into a reason to visit
retail.body: Place an offer at your door with a tight claim radius. It can only be taken by someone standing there, so the redemption you see is a person who came in, not an ad someone scrolled past.

events.body: Festivals, matches and conferences become a temporary layer of assets that expire when the event does. Attendance is what unlocks them, so the reward reaches the people who actually turned up.

Wide radii for grounds, tight ones for stages and stands

token.label: Token & NFT projects
token.title: Distribute to people, not to wallets

summary.title: A protocol for things that exist in a place

blocks.text: The internet made every digital object available everywhere at once. That was the point, and it worked. But it also stripped digital things of the one property that makes physical things feel valuable: being somewhere in particular. A concert ticket matters because it admits you to a room. A landmark matters because you have to travel to it.

Seekprotocol puts location back into digital assets. A token, an NFT, or a reward can be issued to a set of coordinates rather than to a wallet, and it stays there until someone physically stands within its radius and proves it. We call that proof of location, and it is the primitive the rest of the protocol is built on.

The consumer surface is **Seekprotocol**, a mobile app on iOS and Android that renders these assets in augmented reality. You walk, your phone shows what is nearby, and you collect what you find. Underneath, settlement happens on whichever chain the asset already lives on, against a single requirement: transaction costs low enough that picking up a small reward does not cost more than the reward is worth.
The short version: we make digital assets that can only be claimed from a specific place, verify that someone was actually there, and settle it on-chain in under a second for a fraction of a cent.
What this document covers

Sixteen chapters, in four movements. The first three set out the problem and the primitive that answers it. Chapters four to seven are the machine: how a claim travels, how the layers fit, and what the app does with them. Eight to eleven are the economy, from who pays for placement through to who decides the parameters. The last five are the things a whitepaper usually leaves out, which are the attacks, the privacy cost, the regulatory position and the honest limits.

Several figures are playable. The verification model, the claim timeline, the catch roll and the budget calculator all run the arithmetic the protocol runs, with the same constants, so you can disagree with the design rather than with a diagram of it.

problem.title: Attention is cheap online and expensive in the street

blocks.text: Two groups have a problem that turns out to be the same problem viewed from opposite ends.
Brands and venues cannot buy footfall

Digital advertising can put an image in front of someone in milliseconds. It cannot get them to walk three streets over. Conversion from an impression to a physical visit is the weakest link in the entire retail and events funnel, and it is measured badly, usually by asking people at the till whether they saw an ad.

The industry's answer has been modelling. Panels of opted-in devices are extrapolated to a population, and the resulting store-visit figure is reported alongside impressions and clicks as though it came from the same kind of counter. It did not. One number is an event and the other is an estimate, and campaigns are judged on the estimate.
Crypto projects cannot find real users

Airdrops are the standard tool for distribution, and they are farmed. A wallet costs nothing to create, so any reward that can be claimed by a wallet will be claimed by thousands of wallets belonging to a handful of people. Projects respond with ever more elaborate eligibility rules, which mostly filter out ordinary users while sophisticated farmers adapt.

Both problems dissolve if you can prove a human being was in a specific place at a specific time. Footfall becomes measurable because arrival is the event being recorded. Airdrop farming becomes expensive because a wallet is free but travel is not, and nobody is in forty cities at once.

blocks.text: Why this is buildable now and was not before

Three things had to arrive at once. Phones had to carry dual-frequency GNSS, depth-aware cameras and hardware-backed attestation as standard rather than as flagship features. Settlement had to get cheap enough that a reward worth a few cents survives being moved, which ruled out every chain until fees fell below a cent. And people had to be willing to point a camera at a street and see something rendered into it, which a decade of AR in games has quietly settled.

distribution.title: Why paid reach cannot deliver a real person

blocks.text: The previous chapter said two groups have the same problem. This one is about the tool both of them reach for first, and why it fails in a way that spending more does not fix.
Every metric on the market is a proxy

An impression, a click, a view, a follow, a wallet address: not one of these is a person. Each is a signal that correlates with a person under conditions the seller of the signal controls. Once the reward for producing the signal exceeds the cost of producing it without a person, it gets produced without a person, and the correlation the whole market is priced on quietly detaches from the thing it stood in for.

blocks.text: Filters do not restore the signal

The standard response is eligibility rules: minimum balances, prior activity, snapshot windows, captchas, device fingerprints. Each one raises the cost of a fake claim by some amount and the cost of a real claim by some other amount, and the ratio between those two is the only thing that decides whether the filter helped. In practice the sophisticated farmer absorbs the cost and the ordinary user gives up, so the filters end up selecting for the population they were built to exclude.

Presence is not a better filter. It is a different kind of thing, because the cost it imposes is not computational. It cannot be parallelised across a rack, it does not fall as hardware gets cheaper, and there is no residential proxy for a street.

The useful question about any anti-fraud measure is not how much it costs an attacker, it is how much it costs an attacker relative to an honest user. Presence is the only signal on the list where that ratio does not move in the attacker's favour over time.
The publisher still owns the ask

Verifying that someone was somewhere says nothing about what they should have to do while they are there, and the protocol deliberately declines to decide. A claim can be gated on a follow, a signup, a scan of a product on the shelf, a mint at the coordinate, a purchase at the till, or on nothing beyond arrival. The verification underneath is identical in every case, which means a publisher can change the ask between campaigns without changing anything about the guarantee.

This matters for a reason that is easy to miss. A distribution channel that dictates the call to action only fits the campaigns it was designed for, and every publisher outside that shape has to bend their offer to the channel. What is being sold here is the evidence, not the funnel.
What this does not solve

A verified arrival is evidence that a device was at a coordinate, not that the person holding it wanted to be there or will ever come back. Somebody paid to walk past a door is a real arrival and a poor customer. The protocol makes the arrival expensive to fake and simple to count. Whether it was worth buying is still a marketing question, and no chain answers it.
Proof of location is the claim that a given device was inside a given radius during a given window, made credible enough that something of value can be released on the strength of it.

No single signal is trustworthy on its own. Raw GPS can be spoofed by any rooted device with a mock location provider. So the protocol scores a claim across several independent signals and requires the combination to be coherent, because faking one signal is easy and faking all of them consistently is not.
Signals we combine

items: **GNSS fix**, the raw satellite position with its reported accuracy, plus the constellation and satellite count, which spoofers frequently get wrong.
**Ambient radio**, the set of nearby Wi-Fi SSIDs and cell towers, matched against what the protocol expects to see at those coordinates. Radio environments are hard to fabricate and change slowly.
**Device attestation**, Play Integrity on Android and DeviceCheck or App Attest on iOS, confirming the app is genuine and the OS is not compromised.
**Motion continuity**, the accelerometer trace between the previous confirmed position and this one. A claim that you moved 400 km in 90 seconds without a matching motion profile is rejected.
**Temporal plausibility**, where arrival times are checked against the travel time implied by your last confirmed location.

blocks.text: Each signal contributes to a confidence score. Assets set the score they require: a low-value quest reward might accept a moderate score, while a high-value drop at a ticketed event can demand device attestation and a matching radio environment. Claims below the threshold are refused, and repeated refusals from one device raise the threshold for that device.
The goal is not perfect proof, which is unobtainable on consumer hardware. It is to make forgery cost more than the reward is worth, the same standard that keeps card payments workable.
Why the signals are weighted rather than required

A rule that demands every signal is a rule that refuses honest users. Underground stations lose GNSS. New buildings have radio environments the map has never seen. A phone two OS versions behind can fail attestation for reasons that have nothing to do with fraud. Weighting lets an asset say how much evidence its value deserves, and lets an honest claim survive one bad signal without letting a forged claim survive four.

lifecycle.title: What actually happens when you claim something

blocks.text: The previous chapter describes the evidence. This one follows a single claim from the moment you reach for an asset to the moment it is in your wallet, because the order of operations is where most of the design decisions live.
The boundary that matters

Look at where the stages change machine. Everything sensitive happens in the first three: the position, the radio scan, the motion trace, the attestation. None of it leaves your phone in raw form. What crosses to the verifier is a signed claim, and what crosses from the verifier to the chain is a signed attestation that the claim met its threshold.

This is why verification is off-chain. It is not a scaling compromise. Putting the scoring on-chain would mean publishing the inputs, and the inputs are a description of where you are standing and what wireless networks are around you.
What happens when it fails

items: **Below threshold**: the claim is refused, the asset stays on the map, and nothing is written to the chain. The refusal is recorded against the device.
**Repeated refusals**: the required score for that device rises. A device that has failed six claims in an hour is not treated like one that has failed none.

**Settlement failure**: the claim is held and retried rather than dropped. An asset that has been won and not delivered is a bug that costs trust, so the queue is designed to step a stuck payout aside rather than block the ones behind it.
**Expiry mid-claim**: assets carry a window, and a claim that arrives after it closes is refused even at a perfect score. The window is part of the asset, not a network condition.

blocks.text: A claim is a lock, not a lookup. Two people reaching for the last unit of an asset at the same moment must not both be told they got it, so the check takes the lock before it decides anything.
The protocol is four layers. Each one can be reasoned about, and replaced, on its own.

The separation matters most at the boundary between location and settlement. Location verification is probabilistic and happens off-chain, because it depends on sensor data that has no business being public. What reaches the chain is a signed attestation that a claim met its threshold, not your movement history.
What is stored, and where

items: **On-chain**: asset definitions, their coordinates and radii, claim records, and token transfers. Public and permanent.
**Off-chain**: raw sensor readings, radio fingerprints, and device attestations. Retained only as long as needed to score a claim and resolve disputes, then discarded.
**On device**: your position history and AR anchor data. It stays on your phone unless you explicitly share it.

blocks.text: Why the settlement layer is not fixed

The requirement is unusual for a chain: very high transaction count, very low value per transaction, and a confirmation fast enough that a person standing in the street does not notice it. Someone picking up a reward worth twenty cents cannot pay ten cents to receive it, and will not stand still for thirty seconds waiting. That rules out a lot of the field on cost and the rest on latency. It rules them out as a requirement, though, not as a choice of chain made once and built around.

So settlement is configuration. A network is a row carrying its own endpoint, explorer and native token; an asset carries the networks it exists on, with its contract address and decimals on each; and a wallet is one of two address families rather than one per chain, since every EVM network shares an address. A publisher funds a campaign in the token they already hold and the claim settles where that token lives. Adding a network is a row, not a release.

The trade is worth stating. Chains stop, and a chain that stops means claims that queue. Settlement is treated as a step that can fail and be retried rather than one that always succeeds, which is the right design on any network and not optional on a fast one. Spreading across several does not remove that risk. It stops one network's outage from being the whole protocol's outage, which is a smaller claim and the honest one.
What runs where

blocks.text: Seekprotocol is where the protocol becomes something a person can use without knowing any of the above. It opens to a map of what is nearby, and holding up the camera renders those assets in place through the AR engine.
What the app does

items: **Discover**, a live map of drops, quests and events within walking distance, filtered by what you actually care about.
**Collect**, where you point the camera, see the asset anchored in the world, reach out and take it. Settlement happens in the background.
**Guide**, an AI companion that reads your surroundings through the camera and suggests routes, explains what you are looking at, and adapts to how you play.
**Hold**, a built-in wallet created from a social login, so a first-time user is not asked to write down a seed phrase before they can pick anything up.

blocks.text: The onboarding constraint drives more design decisions than any other. Most people who will ever use Seekprotocol have never held a private key. If the first thirty seconds involve the word 'mnemonic', they leave. So the wallet is created silently and can be exported later by anyone who wants custody.
The walk to the drop

Assets sit tens to a couple of hundred metres away, which is a distance where a map is enough and a route is overkill. Marking a spawn draws a straight line from you to it. The line is dashed deliberately: it is a bearing, not a route, it knows nothing about buildings, and over that distance the bearing usually is the walk. It clears itself once you are inside catching range, where the ring takes over.
Spawns expire within the hour. That is a game decision with a protocol consequence: a marker restored on the next launch would point at nothing, so the app does not persist one.
Anchoring, and what AR is for here

The camera pass is not decoration and it is not the verification either. It does two things. It puts the asset at a believable place in the world so that reaching for it is an action rather than a button press, and it gives the motion signal something to be consistent with, because a person walking around an anchored object moves like a person and a spoofer holding a phone still does not.

A protocol that pays for arrival still needs a reason for the first arrival. Nobody walks four streets for a mechanism. The game layer is the demand side of the network, and it is designed with the same honesty as the verification: the odds are published, they are computed on the server, and the client is never asked what happened.
The catch

Reaching an asset does not hand it to you. A charge ring runs while you hold the tap, and the quality of that charge feeds a multiplier. Then the server rolls. You get two attempts on a spawn, and the retry is worth 0.65 of the first, which is the number that makes a second chance feel like a second chance rather than a consolation.
The terms nobody usually publishes

Most games hide the modifiers. There is no reason to here, because the interesting property is that skill nudges and never decides. The charge ring is a multiplier between 0.85 and 1.0, so a perfect tap on a legendary is still a legendary, and a fumbled tap on a common is still probably a common.

items: **Level bonus**, a flat 0.3 points of chance per player level, across ten levels from Seeker to Legend.
**Cold streak**, a pity timer worth 2 points per consecutive miss and capped at 12, which applies to the retry as well as across coins.
**Streak penalty**, 4 points per consecutive success on the same coin and capped at 20, so farming one spawn point gets worse rather than better.
**Clan bonus**, capped at 5 points, earned by the clan rather than the player.
**Power-ups**, bought or won, which multiply the base chance before every other term is added.

blocks.text: The floor is 5% and the ceiling is 95%. Nothing stacks to a guarantee, and nothing stacks to a wall.
Progression, and what it is for

Levels, badges, clans, twelve-hour challenges and weekly goals exist to give the walk a shape longer than one drop. They also do protocol work: a player with a level, a clan and a streak has an account with a history, and a history is expensive to fabricate at scale. Progression is a second cost imposed on the farmer that costs the honest player nothing, because they were going to play anyway.
A location-based network is worthless if the locations are empty. The protocol therefore treats asset placement as a first-class product, not an internal tool.
Three kinds of publisher

items: **Brands and venues** use the business portal to place offers at their own premises and measure who actually arrived. The unit they buy is a verified visit, not an impression.
**Token projects and NFT communities** distribute to people rather than to wallets, using geography as the filter that farming cannot cheaply defeat.
**Event organisers** turn a festival, match or conference into a claimable map for the duration of the event, with assets that expire when it ends.

blocks.text: All three use the same campaign builder: drop a pin, set the radius, choose the asset and quantity, set the confidence threshold and the window, fund it, publish. No integration work, and no contract to write.
For a venue, the metric that matters is cost per verified arrival. It is the first footfall number in digital marketing that is measured at the door rather than inferred from a survey.
The density problem

Supply and demand here are geographic, which makes the usual marketplace advice useless. A thousand assets spread evenly across a country is an empty map everywhere. The same thousand in one city is a reason to leave the house. Placement pricing is therefore weighted by demand for the area rather than being flat, so a saturated high street costs more to hold than a quiet one, and the protocol subsidises the streets that need traffic instead of the ones that already have it.

$SEEK is the settlement and coordination asset of the protocol. It exists because the network has to move value between parties who do not know each other, a brand in one country funding a reward claimed by a stranger in another, and because the cost of placing assets should scale with demand for the places being used.
Utility

items: **Campaign funding**, where publishers denominate and fund rewards in $SEEK.
**Placement fees**, a fee per placed asset, weighted by radius, duration and the demand for that area.
**Staking for priority**, where staked $SEEK raises a publisher's placement priority when several campaigns compete for the same coordinates.
**Rewards**, with the majority of protocol fees flowing back to the people doing the walking.
**Governance**, covering parameter changes, treasury allocation and the confidence thresholds for high-value claims.

An allocation chart says who holds what and nothing about when. The schedule below is the more useful figure, because the risk in a token is rarely the split, it is the cliff.

The design intent is that fee flow tracks real activity rather than speculation: the protocol earns when assets are placed and claimed, which only happens when someone is willing to pay for a verified visit.
What the token deliberately does not do

items: It does not fix a rate between a caught game unit and a token. The game values a catch; the market values the token; the protocol does not pretend to bridge the two.
It is not required to play. Catching, XP and challenges are free, and a player who never touches the token still generates the arrivals a publisher is paying for.
It does not gate placement behind a minimum holding. Staking buys priority when campaigns compete, not the right to publish at all.

revenue.title: How the protocol earns, and from whom

blocks.text: A whitepaper that describes a token and not a business is describing half a system. There are two revenue lines and they come from opposite sides of the network, which is deliberate: neither side alone would keep it running.
Placement, paid by publishers

The primary line. A publisher funds the rewards and pays a placement fee on top, weighted by how much ground the asset holds, for how long, and how contested that ground is. This is the fee that scales with the value the network creates, because it is charged against the thing publishers are actually buying, which is arrival.
The pass and the shop, paid by players

Optional, and bounded on purpose. A seasonal pass runs for ninety days and tilts spawn weighting towards rarer coins, with a weekly rare claim and a boost included. Individual boosts are sold separately: a rare boost, a spawn magnet, an XP multiplier, or a bundle of all three.
Core catching, XP, challenges and platform achievements stay free, permanently. A paid tier that gates the loop would break the only thing publishers are buying, which is people turning up.
Why the split is the right shape

Player spending is elastic, seasonal and capped by how much a person will pay for a hobby. Publisher spending is a marketing line item, judged against a cost per arrival that has a real alternative to be compared with. The first keeps the lights on early, when there are more players than campaigns. The second is what the business becomes, and it only works if the first never degrades into pay-to-win, because a network of paying players who all catch everything reports arrivals that are worth nothing to the venue.

This protocol has an unusually large number of tunable constants: radius bounds, confidence thresholds, placement fee weighting, the share of fees returned to seekers, and the catch ladder itself. Each of them is a policy decision dressed as a configuration value, and pretending otherwise is how protocols end up governed by whoever last edited a file.
The staged position, honestly stated

Governance is not live. Parameters today are set by the core team and changed through migrations that are recorded and reviewable. We are not going to describe that as decentralised, because it is not.

The reason for the delay is not reluctance. Voting on an economy with no volume is theatre: turnout is low, a handful of holders decide, and the decisions being made are about parameters nobody has enough data to judge. Governance becomes meaningful when there is real fee flow, because then a parameter change has a measurable consequence someone can argue about.
What will be governed, and what will not

items: **Governed**: fee weighting, the seeker share of protocol fees, treasury allocation, radius bounds, and the confidence thresholds available to high-value assets.
**Governed with a delay**: anything that changes the value of assets already placed. A campaign funded under one fee schedule should finish under it.
**Not governed**: the privacy commitments in chapter thirteen. Retention limits and the refusal to publish movement data are not parameters, and a vote is not a legitimate way to weaken them.
**Not governed**: individual claim outcomes. A refused claim is a matter for dispute resolution, not a ballot.

blocks.text: A governance system that can vote away its own users' privacy is not a safeguard, it is an attack surface with a quorum.

security.title: Attacks, limits, and what we do not claim

blocks.text: A protocol that pays people for being somewhere invites people to lie about being somewhere. Being specific about the attacks is more useful than asserting the system is secure.
Attacks we defend against

items: **GPS spoofing**, mitigated by requiring the radio environment and motion trace to corroborate the fix, and by device attestation that detects tampered OS builds.
**Sybil farming**, mitigated by the physical cost of travel and by per-device claim limits within a radius and time window.
**Relay attacks**, where a real device at the location signs for a remote user, mitigated by binding attestation to the app instance and the session, and by rate-limiting claims per device.
**Emulator farms**, mitigated by attestation, which emulators fail, and by motion traces that are statistically distinguishable from real walking.
**Client-declared spawns**, prevented rather than mitigated: only the server announces what exists and where, so a modified client can lie about what it sees and gain nothing.
**Double claims**, prevented by taking a lock before the claim is evaluated, so two people reaching for the last unit cannot both be told they got it.

blocks.text: Limits we accept

A sufficiently determined attacker with modified hardware and physical presence at one location can extract more value from that location than an honest user would. We bound the damage with per-location caps rather than pretending it is impossible. Indoor positioning remains materially less accurate than outdoor, so indoor assets use wider radii and lean harder on radio fingerprinting. And no consumer device can prove a human rather than a device was present: a phone in a delivery van still moves like a phone in a pocket.
Risks that are not attacks

items: **Platform dependency**. Attestation is Apple's and Google's to give. A policy change at either could weaken the strongest signal in the stack overnight, and there is no version of this that routes around the operating system.
**Chain availability**. A halted chain means queued claims. The protocol retries rather than drops, but a person standing in the street does not experience a retry as success.

**Physical safety**. Rewarding people for going places puts people in places. Assets are placed at road junctions rather than inside building footprints, high-value drops avoid private property, and the app carries a safety notice. This is a design constraint, not a disclaimer.

blocks.text: We are building an economic deterrent, not a cryptographic guarantee. Where the two are confused, users get hurt.

privacy.title: Location data is the most sensitive data there is

blocks.text: A record of where someone goes reveals their home, their work, their health, their religion and their relationships. Building a network on location claims means accepting responsibility for that, and the responsible design is to hold as little of it as possible.

items: Continuous tracking is never required. The app asks for a position when you attempt a claim, not in the background.
Raw sensor and radio data is used to score a claim and then discarded on a short retention clock.
What is written on-chain is that a claim at a public coordinate succeeded, the same information as a shop knowing someone redeemed a voucher.
Your movement history stays on your device. The protocol does not need it and does not want it.
Publishers receive aggregate counts, never individual traces.

blocks.text: The problem we have not solved

Because claim records are public and permanent by nature of the chain, a determined observer can correlate claims made by the same wallet across locations. That is a genuine weakness and it is inherent to settling on a public ledger. Users who want to avoid it should use separate wallets for separate contexts, and the app makes that easy rather than burying it, but a default that requires the user to know about the problem is not a fix.
The honest summary: we minimise what we hold, we do not sell what we hold, and there is one correlation attack against the public record that we can reduce but not eliminate.
Three regimes touch this protocol at once, which is unusual and worth being explicit about rather than leaving to a footnote.
Data protection

Location is special category adjacent under most modern data protection law, and the protocol is built to the strictest reading rather than the most convenient one. Position is collected for a stated purpose at the moment of a claim, retained only as long as scoring and dispute resolution require, and never combined into a movement profile. Where a regime grants deletion rights, the off-chain record can be deleted; the on-chain claim record cannot, which is a limitation of the ledger and is disclosed rather than glossed.
Token classification

$SEEK is designed as a utility and coordination asset, and the utility described in chapter nine is real rather than decorative. That is a design position, not a legal conclusion. Classification differs by jurisdiction, changes over time, and is not something a whitepaper can settle by asserting it. Availability is therefore restricted where local rules require it.
Rewards, chance and the line into gambling

The catch involves a roll, which puts it near a line that varies by country. Two properties keep it on the right side in most regimes and are held deliberately: participation costs nothing, and the paid items adjust odds and rates rather than being wagers with a variable payout. A pass buys weighting and a boost buys a multiplier; neither is a stake that can be lost. Where a jurisdiction reads it differently, the paid tier is withheld rather than argued with.
